Name: compositional_mechanism_probing
Title: Do Scientific Foundation Models Compose Mechanisms? Probing for Additive vs. Interacting Representation of Combined Scientific Effects
Short Hypothesis: Scientific mechanisms combine according to known composition rules: some effects add (e.g., independent additive free-energy contributions of distant mutations, additive substituent contributions in additive Hammett series), while others interact non-additively (epistasis between contacting residues, saturation/coupling effects). We hypothesize that a foundation model with genuine mechanistic understanding will represent combined stimuli in a way whose internal geometry mirrors the true composition rule — the representation of a two-factor stimulus will be approximately the vector sum of single-factor representations when the true effect is additive, and will deviate from the sum in a direction/magnitude that tracks the true interaction term when the effect is non-additive. Whether a model's representational composition matches the scientifically-correct composition rule is a read-only diagnostic of mechanistic understanding that predicts the model's accuracy on unseen factor combinations.
Related Work: Prior interpretability of scientific foundation models tests whether single concepts, laws, exponents, conservation quantities, relational ontologies, validity domains, causal directions, or mechanistic routes are encoded (BERTology-Meets-Biology; SAE protein-feature reviews; universally-converging-matter representations; and my prior proposals). None test whether the model represents the *composition rule* by which two mechanisms combine — i.e., whether representational algebra (does rep(A+B) = rep(A)+rep(B)?) matches the scientifically-established additive-vs-interacting structure. Word-embedding analogy work showed linear additive composition for general semantics, and mutational epistasis is a well-studied biological phenomenon, but no work asks whether a scientific FM's representation geometry reproduces the correct additive-vs-epistatic composition of mechanisms and whether that predicts combination-generalization. Our contribution is a novel read-only test of compositional representational algebra grounded in known scientific composition rules, distinct from all prior single-concept, single-law, or single-route probing.
Abstract: A powerful feature of scientific reasoning is compositionality: knowing how two mechanisms combine into a joint effect. Crucially, science tells us *how* they combine — sometimes additively (independent, distant contributions), sometimes with a specific interaction term (epistasis between contacting residues, saturation when a resource is limiting, coupled substituent effects). We ask whether foundation models for biology, chemistry, and materials internally represent these composition rules, or whether they fit joint outcomes without capturing whether effects add or interact. We introduce Compositional-Mechanism Probing, a read-only framework. For each of ~10 combinable mechanism pairs with a known additive-or-interacting ground truth, we extract representations of single-factor stimuli (A alone, B alone), a neutral baseline, and the combined stimulus (A+B). We test whether the representational composition residual — rep(A+B) minus [rep(A)+rep(B)-baseline] — is near zero for truly additive pairs and non-zero for interacting pairs, and whether its magnitude and sign track the true interaction term measured experimentally (e.g., double-mutant epistasis from deep mutational scans). We define a Compositional-Fidelity Score aggregating additivity error for additive pairs and interaction-tracking correlation for interacting pairs, benchmarked against randomly-initialized and shuffled controls. We validate that high compositional fidelity predicts better model accuracy on held-out factor combinations. Applied to open protein (ESM-2), molecular (ChemBERTa/MolFormer), and materials models, the framework yields a cheap, reproducible audit of whether scientific models know not just individual mechanisms but how they combine.
Experiments: 1. Combinable-pair curation (~10 pairs with known additive-or-interacting ground truth): proteins -- pairs of point mutations from double-mutant deep mutational scans (MegaScale/large DMS with measured single and double ddG), split into additive pairs (spatially distant residues, near-additive measured double-mutant effect) and epistatic pairs (contacting residues, large measured interaction term); combinations of a stabilizing and destabilizing mutation. Chemistry -- pairs of substituents on a scaffold where additive Hammett/free-energy contributions hold vs. ortho/steric or resonance-coupled pairs that interact (annotated reaction/property datasets); solubility from lipophilicity + H-bonding groups. Materials -- co-substitution/doping effects on bandgap that are additive vs. those that couple. Each pair provides measured single-factor effects, the combined effect, and thus an experimental interaction term. 2. Stimulus construction: for each pair build a neutral baseline input, single-factor inputs (A, B), and the combined input (A+B), matched in all other respects. 3. Models: ESM-2 (8M-650M) for protein pairs, ChemBERTa/MolFormer for chemistry pairs, a public materials/crystal encoder for materials pairs; extract pooled and site-local representations at all layers. 4. Composition residual: compute r_comp = rep(A+B) - [rep(A) + rep(B) - rep(baseline)] at each layer; report its norm normalized by the single-factor effect norms. Additive pairs should have small residual norm; interacting pairs larger. 5. Interaction tracking: for interacting pairs, regress the projected residual (its component along the model's outcome-prediction direction, obtained by probing the output on representations) against the experimentally measured interaction term across many pairs; report correlation/R^2 and sign agreement. 6. Compositional-Fidelity Score (CFS): combine (i) low normalized residual for additive pairs, (ii) high residual for interacting pairs, and (iii) correlation between residual projection and measured interaction term, per domain and layer. 7. Controls: (a) randomly-initialized-model null, (b) shuffled-pairing null (pair A's rep with an unrelated B's measured interaction), (c) output-only baseline testing whether the model's *predicted* combined outcome already recovers additivity/interaction even when internal residual does not (separating 'gets the joint answer' from 'encodes the composition rule'), and (d) a surface-feature baseline checking that additivity/interaction is not trivially readable from token overlap. 8. Combination-generalization validation: hold out the combined (A+B) examples during any probe fitting and test whether per-pair CFS predicts the model's accuracy at predicting held-out combined outcomes (Spearman across pairs/models), i.e., does correct compositional geometry translate into correct combination extrapolation. 9. Scaling analysis: track CFS across model sizes to test whether compositional structure emerges with scale. Metrics: normalized composition-residual norm, residual-vs-interaction correlation, sign agreement, CFS, CFS-vs-combination-generalization correlation, and margins over all controls. Deliverable: an open combinable-mechanism benchmark and per-model Compositional-Fidelity leaderboard across public scientific models.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Vector additivity in representation space is a strong assumption; even a mechanistically-correct model might encode composition nonlinearly, so a large residual for a truly additive pair could be a false negative. We mitigate by testing composition in probe-standardized outcome-relevant subspaces (not raw residual stream) and adding a learned-nonlinear-composition robustness check, treating linear additivity as one hypothesis rather than a requirement. 2. Clean single/double-factor measured data with an interaction term is richest in protein DMS and additive chemistry series and sparser in materials, which may restrict materials to qualitative tests. 3. Surface-feature confounds (combined inputs are lexically the union of single inputs) could inflate residuals; the surface-feature and shuffled-pairing controls guard against this. 4. Distinguishing additive from interacting pairs experimentally requires reliable double-factor measurements; we restrict to datasets with measured single and combined effects and adequate replication. 5. The combination-generalization link is correlational; we report it as validation evidence, complemented by per-pair qualitative analysis. 6. Findings are pair- and model-specific, but this diagnostic specificity is the intended output, and the interaction-tracking and generalization validations make the compositional signal actionable rather than purely descriptive.
